source.title: Phenomenology of Double Descent in Finite-Width Neural Networks
source.authors: Sidak Pal Singh; Aurélien Lucchi; T. Hofmann; B. Schölkopf

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies double descent in finite-width neural networks and measures test loss and Hessian eigenvalues across network sizes, using its own influence-function analysis and experiments rather than the original claim's prescribed comparisons.
record.gate_note: The experiments directly measure population/test loss and Hessian properties over network-size sweeps. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results. Reported figure values without textual numeric values are retained as figure-only measurements.
record.test_reason: The cross-entropy width sweep measures training and test classification error directly. Appendix C.1 states that models near interpolation attain 100% training accuracy, and Figure 3 reports a test-error peak followed by the second descent. This bears on V2 independently of the paper's Hessian analysis. A peak at interpolation does not itself challenge V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the conclusion. More precisely, the authors derive an influence-function population-risk expression and an assumption-dependent lower bound inversely related to the smallest nonzero Hessian eigenvalue. They establish asymptotic MSE double-descent behavior under additional assumptions and demonstrate related behavior empirically in small networks. Cross-entropy experiments show a population-loss peak, a weaker classification-error peak, and a vanishing Hessian near interpolation; the proposed explanation involving SGD convergence to zero-Hessian critical points remains a hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: Uses influence-function population-risk bounds, Hessian-spectrum measurements, and network-size sweeps; it does not reproduce the claim versions' interventions or comparison recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss function changes the observed double-descent behavior and interpolation location: MSE shows a peak near p ≈ KN in the reported setting; cross-entropy population loss peaks/diverges near p ≈ n and test error shows a slight peak. The paper also reports differences across MNIST1D, downsampled CIFAR10, and downsampled MNIST.

fits_no_version.finding: Population-loss peaks coincide with small minimum nonzero Hessian eigenvalues; cross-entropy also produces collapse of the broader Hessian spectrum near interpolation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these finite-width networks, population-loss double descent is associated with Hessian spectral changes whose form depends on the loss function.

fits_no_version.finding: The minimum nonzero function-Jacobian covariance eigenvalue at convergence remains within finite factors of its initialization value in the reported sweeps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested eigenvalue ratio stays comparable across initialization and convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Overall and outer-product Hessian summaries coincide at the optimum.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The functional Hessian vanishes at the optimum in the reported experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Redundant input features shift the linear-regression interpolation peak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective input rank, rather than nominal feature count alone, determines interpolation location in these regression examples.

record.problems: The main empirical sweeps are small due to exact Hessian-spectrum computation costs. The MSE double-descent theory relies on assumptions A2–A4; authors describe the lower bound's practical applicability as secondary. Cross-entropy results include figure-based curves and the vanishing-Hessian explanation is presented as a hypothesis. Several plotted values are not numerically reported in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version result rows apply directly. Cited prior-work claims were excluded. Appendices C.9–C.11 include additional figure-based Hessian and linear-regression measurements, but they do not bear on the eight versions and were not separately rowed beyond R8's summarized linear-regression result.

untested.parts: Paired natural-label and fixed-random-label training, including held-out accuracy under random labels.

Classification-error width sweeps on ordinary MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 under the original recipe; the corresponding experiments here report MSE loss. Strict improvement at every successive post-interpolation width is not established by the supplied qualitative descriptions.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and tuning conditions.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: Separate final-epoch and validation-selected best test-classification-error width sweeps. R3 merges them, although their selection conditions matter for assessing V2.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V2. Its Hessian findings do not test V7: unscaled eigenvalues are not magnitude-aware sharpness, and population loss is not the generalization gap. No precise curve values were reconstructed from the extracted figure text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization paired with natural-label generalization and random-label test accuracy.
Whether test error keeps falling as width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold; the paper instead studies double-descent peaks.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.
Large versus small batch comparisons and training-recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness comparisons; the paper measures Hessian eigenvalues, not the version's perturbation measure.
Removing memorized examples and comparing test accuracy.

rows.measure: Population loss, test error, training error, and Hessian eigenvalues
rows.value: Figure only for curves; text says population loss diverges at p ≈ n, while test error shows a slight peak. Near p ≈ n, training loss remains > 1e − 5 after 80,000 epochs, compared with exact 0 at machine precision in half the epochs for networks in the region where test loss diverges.
rows.note: Text describes the direction of the population-loss and test-error patterns; curve values are figure-only.
rows.check: The slight interpolation peak does not make V2 partial: V2 concerns improvement beyond fitting. Separate population loss, classification error, and Hessian measurements. Figure 3 uses validation-selected best test error; Appendix C.3 also reports final-epoch test error. Nonzero cross-entropy training loss must not be interpreted as nonzero training classification error: Appendix C.1 explicitly reports 100% training accuracy near interpolation.

relationships.condition: One-hidden-layer networks on MNIST1D, cross-entropy, SGD, long training; widths beyond interpolation.
relationships.reason: R3 reports a second descent in test classification error beyond its slight interpolation peak; Appendix C.1 confirms 100% training accuracy near interpolation. This supports the post-fitting direction qualitatively.
relationships.display_finding: Classification error declined beyond a slight interpolation peak under validation-based selection; perfect training accuracy did not imply zero cross-entropy loss.
